text.text: Latest dial-ins
The first and last half hour decide how the day goes. Doing them the same way every day means anyone can open or close.
Opening, 45 minutes before doors
Lights, music, door mat out, tables wiped
Espresso machine on (it needs 20 to 30 minutes to heat)
Fridge and walk-in temperatures written down; 41 degrees or below
Grinders filled; first shots pulled to season them
Dial in the house espresso and log it
Batch brew started; cold brew checked
Pastries baked or set out to the day's par
Milk, oat milk, syrups and cups stocked at the bar
Till counted and ready
During the day
Restock cups, lids and milk at quiet moments, not during a rush.
Wipe steam wands after every drink; purge before and after.
Log waste as it happens.
Closing, after the last order
Backflush the espresso machine with cleaner; soak portafilters and baskets
Brush grinders; empty and wipe the hoppers if they hold coffee overnight
Empty and rinse the batch brewer
Wrap, label and date anything kept for the next day; log the rest as waste
Milk and bakery counted for the morning order
Floors swept and mopped; trash and recycling out
Till counted; doors locked; alarm set
Times
If the opener is late
The first person in starts the machine and the oven before anything else; everything else on the list can wait 20 minutes, but a cold machine cannot. Keep the opening list printed by the door.
Who does what
The opener owns the dial-in and the pastry par; the closer owns the clean and the counts. Write their names on the shift plan so it is clear.
Weekly deep clean
Pick the quietest afternoon: pull the fridge out and clean behind it, descale the kettle, wash the syrup pumps, and clean the grinder burrs with grinder cleaning tablets.
Example

The closer counted 3 trays of croissant dough against a par of 6, so the morning order includes three more trays, and the waste log shows 6 unsold croissants, which suggests the par for that weekday is too high.
Every cup should taste the same no matter who makes it. A written recipe, a scale, a timer and a dial-in log make that possible.
The house recipe

cells.text: Sweet, balanced, no sour edge, no bitter finish

text.text: How to dial in
Weigh the dose; level and tamp the same way every time.
Pull a shot; weigh the yield and time it.
Taste it straight.
Adjust one thing at a time:
Log the final dose, yield, time, grind and taste.
When to dial in
At opening, after the rush, and whenever a new bag is opened.
When the weather changes; humidity moves grind.
When a guest says the coffee tastes different.
Milk
Steam to 140 to 150 degrees; never reheat. Stretch less for a flat white than for a latte. Oat milk needs a lower temperature to avoid a burnt taste.
Training a new barista
Day one: watch, clean, learn the bar layout and the menu builds.
Days two to five: espresso only, logging every shot until five in a row are in range.
Week two: milk drinks, then rush shifts with a trainer beside them.
A taste test with the lead before working the bar alone.
Consistency checks
Once a week, the lead tastes a flat white from each barista. Note what to adjust, kindly and specifically.
Example

The Guatemala on its second day ran 25 seconds and tasted thin at 40 grams out. The barista should have cut the yield to 36 grams before changing the grind, and the log now shows that for the next person.
Waste is margin thrown in the bin. Logging it honestly, and ordering to pars, is the cheapest way to make a cafe more profitable.
Logging waste
Every item thrown out goes in the waste log the same shift: what, how many, why, and the cost.
Reasons:
Expired
Spill
Mistake
Quality
Staff meal
Mistakes are not punished; they are counted, so training can fix them.
Reading the log weekly

Par too high for that day
Lower the par for that day
Retrain; post the build at the bar
Held too long or old beans

text.text: Pars and ordering
Count beans, milk, bakery and cups at close; enter
On hand
The
Order?
flag shows what is below par.
Order on a fixed day per vendor, with enough lead time.
Raise a par when you run out twice in a month; lower it when you throw out the same item twice in a week.
Order days
Late or short deliveries
An order still Placed after its arrival date shows under Overdue. Call the vendor the same morning and decide what to swap or take off the board.
Receiving
Check the delivery against the order, look at dates on milk, and put new stock behind old stock. Set the order to
Arrived
with the date.
Example
Unsold croissants appear twice in the last week. The owner drops the croissant par on Mondays from 24 to 18 and watches whether they sell out before 2 pm.
The espresso machine and grinders are the heart of the bar. Daily care keeps the coffee tasting right; scheduled service prevents the breakdown that shuts the cafe.
Daily
Backflush with cleaner at close; plain water backflush mid-day
Purge and wipe steam wands after every drink
Soak portafilters and baskets overnight
Brush grinder chutes; purge after setting changes
Fridge temperatures logged at open and close
Weekly
Remove and clean group gaskets and shower screens
Clean the drip tray and drain
Wipe grinder hoppers with a dry cloth
Descale the kettle and clean the batch brewer
Water
Hard water damages machines faster than anything else. Change the water filter on schedule, often every three to six months, and write the date on the equipment.
Scheduled service
The equipment list shows
Days to service
; anything past due is on the overdue list.
When something breaks
Set the status to
Needs service
or
Out of order
Call the technician; note the call on the machine.
Decide on a workaround: a backup grinder, batch brew only, or bought-in pastries.
Put a short note on the menu board if a drink is off.
Cleaning products
Use the cleaner the machine maker recommends, at the strength on the label. Too much leaves a taste; too little leaves oils that turn rancid and make every shot bitter.
Spare parts on the shelf
Group gaskets, shower screens, a steam wand tip, grinder brushes, a spare portafilter basket, and the technician's number on the wall.
Example
The main grinder is 10 days past its service date and now drifts during the rush. Service is booked; until then the decaf grinder is set up with the house blend as a backup.
A cafe lives on small margins repeated hundreds of times a day. A few cents of waste per drink, or a grinder that drifts, adds up to real money. This workspace keeps those small things visible.

text.text: How the numbers work
Margin per sale
is price minus cost to make. Espresso drinks usually run at 70 to 80 percent margin; food lower.
Stock value
is on hand times cost per unit, so the weekly count shows how much money sits on the shelves.
Value wasted this month
on each menu item adds up its waste log entries.
Your first week
Enter your menu with the build, price and cost to make. Weigh your real recipes, not the ones on the wall.
Enter supplies with pars and cost per unit from your last invoices.
Log every dial-in and every bit of waste from day one.
Add machines with their last service and filter dates.
The daily rhythm
Open:
temperatures logged, espresso dialed in and logged, pastries baked to the par for that day.
After the rush:
check the dial-in again; grinders drift as the hopper empties and the room warms.
Close:
waste logged, machines cleaned, counts for milk and bakery.
Weekly
Count supplies, check what to order, compare waste by item, and look at the dashboard for margin and sales.
Example
After the lunch rush the house blend ran fast and tasted sour at 26 seconds. The barista tightened the grind one step and logged it, and the afternoon shots came back to balanced.
